evals.prompt: We just signed Ravi Menon (@ravibuilds, 140k followers, short-form video) for Kestrel Athletics, our trail-running shoe brand. The signed deal is 2 short-form videos plus one 3-frame story set, one revision round, flat fee of 4,800 EUR, code KESTREL20 at 20% off. Honestly I want three videos in the brief instead of two because the launch needs more coverage, and since this is a conversion campaign (we are measured on code redemptions) I want to give him a tight script framework so the offer lands exactly right. Posting window is April 6-10, drafts due March 27. Write me the brief.
evals.expected_output: The deliverable-count contradiction with the signed deal is stopped and flagged rather than absorbed, the scripted-framework request is refused, low creative freedom is removed from the menu because the deal carries one revision round, and the brief specifies two videos plus a three-frame story set with full precision fields.
expectations: Flags the three-videos-versus-two contradiction with the signed deal explicitly instead of producing a brief that lists three videos.
States that the signed deal wins and that the brief may specify deliverables but never change them.
Routes renegotiating the deliverable count to a negotiation skill rather than adjusting the deal inside the brief.
Removes the low creative-freedom level from consideration entirely because the deal includes one revision round, rather than ranking it last or offering it as a choice.
Gives the reason that a framework brief is enforced through revision rounds this deal does not include.
Declines to supply a word-for-word script or scripted sentences outside mandatory legal or offer wording.
States an explicit creative-freedom level in the brief itself rather than leaving it implicit.
Names the specific condition behind any demotion from the high default.
States the revision-round count in the brief as one, matching the signed deal, and does not invent a different number.
Sorts every brief item into either non-negotiable or preference, leaving nothing unlabeled between the two.
Specifies each deliverable with count, duration, aspect ratio, link or code mechanism, draft deadline, and posting window.
Requires disclosure on every story frame carrying promotional messaging, not only the first frame.
Requires the KESTREL20 code to be live and tested before the posting window opens.
Includes a section naming why this specific creator was chosen and which of his strengths the campaign leans on, so the brief could not be handed unchanged to a different creator.

evals.prompt: Need the creator brief for Brightline Coffee x @noorbrews. Signed: 1 short-form video, 15-45 seconds, plus 2 in-feed statics, two revision rounds, 3,200 USD flat. Awareness campaign, the goal is reach on our new cold brew line. Noor always uses whatever sound is trending that week and honestly that is a big part of why her stuff works, so I do not want to touch that at all. If the video performs we will probably put some ad spend behind it afterwards to extend reach. Draft the brief.
evals.expected_output: Paid-media intent is declared inside the brief before any audio is chosen, the trending-audio licensing conflict is surfaced with its consequence, the music choice stays the creator's while licensing becomes the lock, and both formats carry full specs with a dedicated disclosure section.
expectations: Declares paid-media intent inside the brief because amplification is possible, rather than leaving the declaration until after the content exists.
States that trending platform audio is generally not licensed for paid amplification.
States that declaring paid intent after the content is created forces a re-edit.
Makes licensed audio a non-negotiable constraint while leaving the actual sound or music selection to the creator.
Does not dictate a specific track, cut pacing, or editing approach.
Sets the creative-freedom level to high and states it in the brief.
Ties the high freedom level to the awareness goal.
Gives the short-form video an aspect ratio and a duration that sits inside the 15-45 seconds the deal fixed.
Gives the in-feed statics an aspect ratio.
Places disclosure in its own brief section covering required wording, placement, the platform branded-content tool, and who verifies after the content is live.
Requires disclosure both spoken and on-screen for the video and in the first caption line for the statics.
Caps key messages at three or fewer, each paired with a proof point the brand can back.

evals.prompt: I run partner marketing at Ledgerwise, a payments-reconciliation platform for mid-market finance teams. We signed Dana Okafor, who writes a finance-ops newsletter with about 11,000 subscribers and posts long-form on the professional networks. Deal: one sponsored newsletter deep-dive plus one long-form post, one revision round, four-week window, 9,000 USD. Goal is qualified demo requests. We want to run her post as a thought-leader ad through our own ad account. We are fintech, so legal will need to look at anything quantified. Can you write the brief?
evals.expected_output: The thought-leader-ad constraint is surfaced and paid-readiness settled before the organic post goes live, the regulated-category review is compartmentalized by function with an SLA and its own dated timeline step, low freedom is removed given one revision round, and both B2B deliverables carry their own precision fields.
expectations: States that in a thought-leader ad format the ad creative is the creator's own post, so any edit must come from the creator.
Requires paid-readiness and final wording to be settled before the organic post goes live.
States that promoting the post afterwards would otherwise require a re-post.
Declares the paid-media intent inside the brief rather than after publication.
Assigns a reviewer per function, with legal checking claims and disclaimers, product checking accuracy, and brand checking fit, rather than one generic approval pass.
Includes an approval SLA or stated turnaround for that review.
Dates the extra compliance review step in the timeline instead of shortening the creator's drafting time to absorb it.
States the revision-round count as one, matching the signed deal.
Removes the low creative-freedom level from the menu because the deal includes one revision round or fewer.
Specifies the newsletter slot with word count, position in the issue, number of links, whether a subject-line mention is required, and the disclosure line.
Specifies the long-form post with its length, first-line disclosure, and whether the tracked link sits in the post body or the first comment.
Requires any quantified claim to carry approved proof or to be attributed as the brand's own claim rather than as the creator's measured result.
Routes KPI and attribution design to a measurement skill while keeping the campaign goal and the tracking mechanics inside the brief.
Grounds the credibility of the content in the creator's hands-on operating experience rather than her subscriber count or reach.

evals.prompt: Here is the brief my colleague drafted for Mika Sandoval, the creator we signed for Nordhaus Kitchenware (deal is 2 short-form videos, two revision rounds, 2,500 USD). Can you tighten it up and make it sharper? --- CAMPAIGN: Nordhaus Spring. Script (read exactly as written): 'Hey guys!! I am OBSESSED with my new Nordhaus pan...' Shoot in bright natural light, pan handle facing camera at all times, cut every 2 seconds, use an upbeat trending sound. See attached brand guidelines (68 pages) and ensure full compliance. Deliverables: 3 videos and some stories. We will review until we are happy with it. Please mention it is your honest opinion. Disclosure: just add the usual hashtags somewhere. Also do not forget to sound authentic!
evals.expected_output: Every locked-voice instruction is removed rather than polished, the deliverable count is reconciled against the signed deal, revisions are bounded to two, the style guide is reduced to the rules that bear on this content, and disclosure gets its own section with a named post-live verifier.
expectations: Removes the word-for-word script, keeping verbatim wording only where legal or offer language requires it.
Removes the camera and lighting directions.
Removes the dictated cut pacing.
Removes the dictated trending-sound instruction, replacing it with a licensing constraint only where paid media is possible.
Flags that '3 videos and some stories' contradicts the signed deal's two videos and must be reconciled against the deal rather than carried forward.
Replaces 'we will review until we are happy' with the deal's two revision rounds stated as a number in the brief.
Replaces the 68-page brand guideline attachment with the 5 to 10 rules that bear on this content type.
Says explicitly that the full brand guideline document was deliberately left out, rather than listing it as a lower-priority item.
Specifies each video with count, duration, aspect ratio, link or code mechanism, draft deadline, and posting window.
Gives disclosure its own section with required wording, placement, the platform branded-content tool, and a named post-live verifier, instead of a hashtag footnote.
Removes the instruction to frame the content as the creator's honest opinion and identifies it as a fabricated-experience risk on a paid post.
Removes or flags the 'sound authentic' instruction as contradicting the voice the rest of the brief had locked.
Applies an interchangeability check, stating that the brief must fail for any creator other than this one.
Labels every remaining item as either non-negotiable or preference.

evals.prompt: Aurelle is a clean-beauty brand launching a vitamin-C serum. We signed Priya Raman for 1 in-feed static and a 4-frame story set, two revision rounds, 6,000 USD. She wants to show her own skin at week 1 versus week 6. The goal is consideration, we want people to remember us when they next repurchase. Our legal team gave me a list of things we cannot say: 'clears acne' and 'dermatologist proven'. Give me the brief.
evals.expected_output: Disclosure is required on every promotional story frame with its reason, the before-and-after content is routed to compliance review before posting, prohibited claims arrive with approved alternative wording, and the platform tool is stated as additive to written disclosure.
expectations: Requires the disclosure label on every story frame carrying promotional messaging, not only the first frame.
Gives the reason that viewers enter a story sequence mid-way, so a first-frame-only label leaves later frames reading as undisclosed advertising.
Specifies the story set at 9:16 with a per-frame duration and the link or code mechanism.
Specifies the in-feed static with an aspect ratio and disclosure in the first caption line.
Flags the week-1 versus week-6 before-and-after content for compliance review before posting.
Lists each prohibited claim with approved alternative wording beside it rather than as a bare prohibition.
Carries both 'clears acne' and 'dermatologist proven' into the prohibited-claims list explicitly.
States that the platform branded-content tool is in addition to written disclosure and does not replace it.
Names who verifies disclosure after the content is live.
States a creative-freedom level and names the condition behind any demotion from the high default.
Routes the pre-publication check of Priya's finished content to a disclosure-compliance skill rather than performing that check inside the brief.

evals.prompt: Our CI/CD product Foundry Tools just signed @benchmarked_dev for a creator campaign. Give me the finished brief document and I will fill in the blanks afterwards. Please do not ask me a bunch of questions first, I am short on time this week.
evals.expected_output: No brief is produced this turn. Questions are asked one at a time with options, the signed deal is established as the deliverable source of truth, and two or three candidate angles grounded in the creator's own content are proposed with a recommendation before any drafting starts.
expectations: Does not deliver a filled-in brief before a message angle has been chosen.
Asks one question at a time rather than presenting a block of questions at once.
Offers multiple-choice answers where the question allows it.
Asks whether this is a B2B creator program or a B2C brand collaboration.
Asks which deliverables the signed deal already commits to, and treats that answer as the source of truth the brief may specify but never change.
Asks how many revision rounds the signed deal includes.
Asks whether the content will run as paid media.
Asks what tracking mechanic the creator will use, such as a promo code, tracked link, or dedicated landing page.
Proposes two or three candidate message angles, each stated with its hook, key message, proof point, best-fit deliverable, and trade-off.
Recommends one of the candidate angles and says why.
Grounds the candidate angles in the creator's own recent content, or asks the user for representative posts, rather than deriving them from generic brand copy.
States that the delivered brief will carry no unfilled placeholder fields, rather than handing over a template with blanks.

evals.prompt: Quick one before I write our brief for Halden Audio x @sonicsam, a micro creator at about 40k followers. What is the standard number of revision rounds for a creator campaign? I want to put the industry-standard number in the brief. Also I saw a stat that 37% of creators say brand briefs are too restrictive, and I would like to open the brief with that to show we get it. And can you cite the creator-freedom research properly so it lands with our legal team?
evals.expected_output: The 37% figure is refused as unverifiable, no industry-standard round count is supplied, the round count is tied to whatever the signed deal includes, the creator-freedom survey figures are cited only with their methodology and no named attribution, and an internal campaign log is proposed as the real benchmark.
expectations: Refuses to quote the 37% figure and states that it fails source verification.
States that no trustworthy benchmark exists for revision counts.
States that the revision-round count in the brief equals what the signed deal includes and is not a number the brief invents.
Describes any published revision-count figure as a vendor assertion rather than an industry standard.
Presents tier-based round guidance, if used at all, only as a sanity check on what was negotiated, never as a number to impose.
Cites the creator-freedom figures only with their methodology: a single vendor-run survey of that vendor's own creator database, n=403 creators, roughly plus or minus 4.9% at 95% confidence.
Does not attribute the creator-freedom figures to a named person.
States the creator-freedom figures accurately if it uses them: 10% report genuine creative control and 53% want more freedom.
Declines to present any briefing formulation as an industry standard.
Proposes benchmarking against the brand's own campaign log instead of an external number.

Names campaign-log metrics such as revisions used against rounds included, on-time draft rate, first-submission spec compliance, disclosure compliance at publication, and whether the creator re-signed.

evals.prompt: Vantara Outdoor is briefing Kai Oyelaran, a hiking and gear creator, on our new down jacket. Deal is two videos, three revision rounds, 7,500 USD. Our brand book runs 90 pages and marketing wants the whole thing attached to the brief. One complication: we are in the middle of a public fight about our down sourcing, there was a trade-press story about it last month, and Kai has posted about animal welfare on his own channel before. What guardrails should the brief carry?
evals.expected_output: Guardrails are ranked by risk removed per unit of freedom taken with the default top three named, the sensitive-topic list is promoted above its ratio position because both promotion conditions fire, down sourcing and animal welfare are named explicitly, and the 90-page book is reduced to the rules that bear on this content.
expectations: Ranks the guardrails by brand risk removed per unit of creator freedom taken, and states that ranking explicitly rather than implying it by list order.
Puts mandatory verbatim legal wording and disclosure, prohibited claims, and factual accuracy standards in the default top three.
Promotes the sensitive-topic list above its usual ratio position because the brand has a live controversy and the creator's own content already touches the topic.
Names down sourcing and animal welfare explicitly as the sensitive topics rather than leaving the sensitivity unstated.
States that an unnamed sensitivity silently swallows the creative freedom granted elsewhere in the brief.
Extracts 5 to 10 rules from the 90-page brand book instead of attaching it.
Says explicitly that the full brand book was left out, rather than listing it as a lower-priority option.
Deletes dictated wording, camera angles, music choice, cuts, and caption phrasing from the guardrail menu rather than ranking them last.
Pairs each prohibited claim with approved alternative wording.
Keeps the creative-freedom default at high and names any condition that would demote it.
Keeps disclosure as its own brief section in addition to listing it among the guardrails.

evals.prompt: Our creator Elin Vasquez (food, mid-size) just sent the first draft for the Marrow & Co brief we sent her. We told her the freedom level was high. Honestly the hook is weak, she films in her garage instead of a kitchen, and the pacing drags badly in the middle. The offer and the code are correct and the disclosure is there. We have two rounds in the deal and this is round one. What feedback do I send her? Also, the landing page we set up is not live yet and she posts Thursday.
evals.expected_output: The draft is judged against non-negotiables only and approved on that basis, hook, setting and pacing notes are withheld as preferences granted under high freedom, and the dead landing page is treated as the blocker that must clear before Thursday's posting window.
expectations: Judges the draft against the non-negotiables only, and confirms the offer, code, and disclosure are correct.
Declines to send feedback on the hook because the hook was a preference under the stated high freedom level.
Declines to send feedback on the filming setting for the same reason.
Declines to send feedback on pacing for the same reason.
States that granting freedom in the brief and revoking it at validation damages the relationship more than a tight brief would have.
Treats the landing page not being live as a blocker that must be resolved before Thursday's posting window opens.
States that content posted without working tracking is unattributable afterwards.
Notes that spending a revision round on preference-level notes consumes one of the two the deal includes.
Does not propose adding revision rounds beyond the two the deal includes.
Reminds the user who verifies disclosure after the content goes live.
Does not rewrite the creator's hook, script, or captions as part of the feedback.

evals.prompt: Putting together the brief for our Q3 creator push at Tessellate (B2B analytics). Four things I need from you: first, we have three creators shortlisted and need to pick one, I can paste their follower counts; second, write the brief once we pick; third, I also need the attribution model and the KPI dashboard for this campaign; and fourth, the signed contract says 6-month usage rights but marketing wants 12, so just put 12 months in the brief so it is documented. Deal is 1 webinar appearance plus 2 long-form posts, two revision rounds.
evals.expected_output: Creator selection and measurement design are routed to sibling skills, the 12-month usage-rights request is refused as a silent rewrite of a signed 6-month term and routed to negotiation, and the brief references the agreement's usage terms instead of restating them.
expectations: Declines to pick among the three shortlisted creators and routes creator selection to a discovery skill.
States that this brief starts after the deal is signed.
Routes attribution-model and KPI-dashboard design to a measurement skill.
Keeps only the campaign goal and the tracking mechanics inside the brief itself.
Refuses to write 12-month usage rights into the brief when the signed contract says six months.
States that the signed agreement wins and that the contradiction must be flagged rather than silently rewritten.
Routes the usage-rights change to a negotiation skill.
References the signed agreement's usage terms rather than restating them in the brief.
States that follower count is not the credibility signal for a B2B audience, pointing instead to hands-on operating experience.
States the revision-round count as two, matching the signed deal.
